svg.title: Ray time on the head and worker pods
svg.text: Ray on the head and workers: workflow, functions, line numbers and measured times
Code: ej-prj-i4-5 1266cccd2 (no Ray dashboard), Ray 2.56.1. One sky launch (run 6 of 6) on 6 pods on k8s/kind-skypilot, one echo. Clock times are seconds from the start of sky launch.
The letter beside a time says where it comes from. Time ranges cover the 5 worker pods. The timeline is at the bottom.
timers in each Python process, in the trace image
timestamps in Ray's own logs: gcs_server.out, raylet.out, the agents' logs
Ray event stats, earlier sky exec trace (20261104-ray-api-trace)
ray start, GCS, raylet, agents; no dashboard
ray start, raylet, per-job Ray workers
Almost all Python start and imports for the ray CLI. GCS itself takes
tens of ms. Workers wait for this port.
No dashboard to wait for: start_api_server returns at once, so ray start
goes straight on to the raylet. With the dashboard this was 2.4–2.6 s.
Raylet waits for its two agents → registered
Both agents are now mostly Python start and imports. The runtime env
Sets when the Ray wait begins. With the offline wheel install, runtime
setup was 1.4–2.0 s across 6 launches: no stalls.
Set by the head's imports. ray start begins within 0.07 s of GCS
Poll for the head's node record
Now short: the head registers about 1.5 s after GCS starts, so most
workers find it on the first or second poll (1 median).
Raylet: connect to its own plasma store
A fixed 1 s sleep when the first connect races the store thread and
fails. It hit 3 of 5 workers here, 13 of 36 raylets in 6 launches, and
the last worker to register in 6 of 6.
Raylet waits for its two agents → registered
No modules to load now: both agents are Python start and imports.
Skylet start, and wait for all 6 nodes
These run together, and the launch waits for both. The lean launcher
keeps skylet well under the Ray wait.
Setup between Ray and the job
SkyPilot, not Ray: two Python commands on the head, mostly imports. Now
the largest gap before the job. Times per step are from the v2 trace;
home directory echo, rsync job script
Largest fixed cost in the job: import sky loads the whole backend,
though the driver uses five modules.
Connect, reserve one bundle per node
GCS asks each raylet to reserve
Waits for new Ray worker processes.
Ray worker process starts, runs check_ip
Submit tasks, wait for each rank
Load the task function, run the command
Includes importing what the task function needs.
After the last Ray call: Ray's shutdown and Python's exit, not broken
Timeline of one sky launch, run 6 of 6 (seconds from the start of sky launch, wall time 23.81 s; 'Workers' rows are medians of 5 pods, raylet rows are single pods)
Durations across all 6 launches (seconds; worker values are medians of 5 pods per launch)
Head: GCS listening → raylet first log (no dashboard wait)
of which runtime env agent, start → listening
Workers: poll for the head's node record
Last worker: plasma store → ObjectManager up
Raylets with the 1 s plasma retry (of 6)

Six sky launch runs on 6 pods, code ej-prj-i4-5 1266cccd2: 0.2 s head-node poll, lean skylet launcher, offline wheel install, and no Ray dashboard. Ray 2.56.1, kind on one machine, so all pods share a clock.

Wall times were 30.0, 22.8, 22.7, 23.7, 23.5, 23.8 s; run 1 is the first launch after a server restart. The timeline is one real launch; the table shows how much each stage varies. There is no comparison or
significance test here: the A/B with and without the dashboard is in bench_results/20261105-no-dashboard-ab/summary.md.

The 1 s plasma retry: the raylet starts the plasma store on a thread, then connects to its socket. If the socket isn't there yet, ConnectSocketRetry sleeps raylet_client_connect_timeout_milliseconds (1000)

before retrying. It hit 13 of 36 raylets, at least one in 6 of 6 launches, and the last worker to register in 6 of 6. It was there with the dashboard too (9 of 36 raylets in the v2 trace), but hidden behind the
dashboard agent wait. A shorter retry setting would also cut the total retry time, so it needs care.

The trace image adds timers to every Python process. Never benchmark latency with it. Who called whom in S rows is inferred from sent and received counts in an earlier trace. Not shown: tasks with setup,
